claim: override_flags_definitions and only_use_override_person_properties are passed through with no is_internal_request gate (unlike detailed_analysis), so any holder of the public project token can substitute an arbitrary flag definition for an arbitrary distinct_id and use /flags as an attacker-chosen predicate oracle over another user's person properties; the per-request info! logging of attacker-controlled filter JSON is a secondary issue.
raw: #1 Critical: `override_flags_definitions` and `only_use_override_person_properties` are reachable with only a public project token — The change gates `detailed_analysis` behind `authentication::is_internal_request(&context)` (`mod.rs:218`) but passes `request.override_flags_definitions` (`mod.rs:196`) and `context.meta.only_use_override_person_properties` (`mod.rs:223`) through with no gate at all. `/flags` is authenticated only by the project API token from the request body, which is public and embedded in every web client. Any caller can therefore replace an existing flag's entire definition in-memory for their own request — and choose the `distinct_id` freely.

claim: model_to_dict cannot emit the non-editable AutoField id, and the Rust FeatureFlag struct requires id with no serde default, so deserialization of the historical override fails, flags.rs warns and keeps the cached flag, and the endpoint silently returns an evaluation of the present-day flag definition labelled as historical.
raw: #2 High: historical flag override never applies — `model_to_dict` omits `id`, so the Rust service rejects it and evaluates the *current* definition — `model_to_dict` only emits fields with `editable=True` and `AutoField` forces `editable=False`. So `flag_dict` has no `id`. The Rust `FeatureFlag` struct requires it — `pub id: FeatureFlagId` with no `#[serde(default)]`. `serde_json::from_value::<FeatureFlag>` therefore fails with `missing field 'id'`, and `flags.rs:177-184` logs a `warn!` and keeps the flag from cache. The request still succeeds, so `POST /test_evaluation` with a `timestamp` returns an evaluation of the flag's present-day definition.

claim: The new test_evaluation action declares required_scopes=["feature_flag:read"] but always returns the person's full person_properties dict for any caller-named distinct_id/person_id, which is a scope escalation past the person:read scope normally required to read person data.
raw: #3 High: `test_evaluation` returns person properties under a `feature_flag:read` scope — The new action declares `required_scopes=["feature_flag:read"]` yet the response body includes `person_properties` — the person's full property dictionary (email, name, and any custom PII), for any `distinct_id`/`person_id` the caller names. `APIScopePermission._get_required_scopes` honours the per-action override, so a personal API key granted only `feature_flag:read` now reads person data that otherwise requires the `person` scope. That is a scope escalation.

claim: this_condition_rollout_excluded is gated on rollout_percentage == 0.0 in every branch, so the ordinary partial-rollout exclusion (properties match, hash out of bucket) reports rollout_excluded: false and emits the false explanation "matched properties but was not evaluated due to an earlier condition matching" even for a single-condition flag.
raw: #4 High: `rollout_excluded` only fires at 0% rollout, so the common rollout exclusion is labelled with a false explanation — `this_condition_rollout_excluded` is gated on `is_zero_rollout = rollout_percentage == 0.0` in every branch (`:679`, `:682`, `:686`). Rollout exclusion happens for any rollout below 100%, so the ordinary case — properties match, user's hash falls outside a partial rollout — reports `rollout_excluded: false` and picks the `all_properties_matched && !condition_matched` branch, emitting "Condition N matched properties but was not evaluated due to an earlier condition matching". For a single-condition flag there is no earlier condition; the statement is simply false.

claim: internal_request_token is read via a raw os.getenv with no Django setting or default, so when INTERNAL_REQUEST_TOKEN is unset the Rust side degrades detailed_analysis to false and returns HTTP 200 with conditions: [] (silently missing the documented analysis), and record_usage no longer short-circuits so the customer is billed for PostHog-initiated test evaluations.
raw: #5 Medium: with `INTERNAL_REQUEST_TOKEN` unset, analysis is silently dropped and the customer is billed for test evaluations — The endpoint always requests `detailed_analysis=True` but passes `internal_request_token=os.getenv("INTERNAL_REQUEST_TOKEN")` — a raw env read with no Django setting and no default, and the Rust side has no default either. When the variable is unset or the two services disagree, `is_internal_request` returns `false`, `mod.rs:218` degrades `detailed_analysis` to `Some(false)`, and the endpoint returns HTTP 200 with `conditions: []`. In the same failure mode `record_usage` no longer short-circuits, so every internal test evaluation increments the team's billable flag-request counter.

claim: The return_debug_info parameter was deleted from build_person_properties_at_time but posthog/api/person.py:1448 still passes return_debug_info=True and unpacks a 4-tuple, so that debug call path raises TypeError and returns HTTP 500; it is the only remaining reference and no test covers it.
raw: #6 Medium: removing `return_debug_info` breaks the existing `point_in_time` person endpoint — The `return_debug_info` parameter was deleted from `build_person_properties_at_time`, but `posthog/api/person.py:1448` still passes `return_debug_info=True` and unpacks a 4-tuple at `:1451-1453`. That call raises `TypeError: build_person_properties_at_time() got an unexpected keyword argument 'return_debug_info'` → HTTP 500. It is the only remaining reference in the repo, and no test covers it. The branch is guarded by `if debug and settings.DEBUG:`, so production is unaffected.

claim: build_condition_analysis calls match_property with person properties only for every filter, so group- and cohort-type filters are evaluated against person properties and always come back false, reporting "Condition N did not match properties" for any flag targeting groups or cohorts; separately, matched: all_properties_matched (:713) is serialized into a field documented as "whether this condition was the one that matched", and rollout-only conditions hard-code all_properties_matched=true so they always report matched: true.
raw: #7 Medium: condition analysis evaluates group/cohort/flag filters against person properties and overloads `matched` — 1. `match_property(property, props, false)` is called for every filter with `props` = merged person properties only. `match_property` is type-agnostic — it looks up `property.key` in whatever map it is given. A `type: "group"` filter is therefore tested against person properties, and a `type: "cohort"` filter is tested against a person property literally named `id`. Both come back `false`... Every flag targeting groups or cohorts gets a wrong analysis. 2. `matched: all_properties_matched` (`:713`) is serialized into a field documented as "Whether this condition was the one that matched"... such a condition always reports `matched: true` even when the flag evaluated to `false`.

claim: find_version_at_timestamp returns version 1 as a guess when no activity-log entry at or before the timestamp carries a version change, and reconstruct_flag_at_version's target_version == 1 branch then returns the flag's current field values with is_historical=True, reporting today's definition as the definition at the requested past time with no error or warning.
raw: #8 Medium: `find_version_at_timestamp` guesses version 1 when no versioned log entry exists, yielding the current definition labelled historical — If no activity-log entry at or before the timestamp carries a `version` change (flags predating version tracking, pruned logs, or entries logged without a version bump) and `timestamp < flag.updated_at`, the function returns `1` — a guess presented as fact. `reconstruct_flag_at_version(flag, 1, ...)` then walks the log, finds no versioned entry to undo, never sets `reached_target`, and takes the `target_version == 1` branch which returns the current field values with `is_historical=True`. The endpoint reports today's filters as the definition at the requested past time.

claim: flag_was_deleted is only updated inside the `if version_after is not None` guard, but the bulk-delete path logs activity="deleted" with no version bump, so bulk-deleted flags are reported as alive for the whole deleted window and the endpoint returns a pre-delete evaluation instead of "did not exist at the specified timestamp", contradicting the documented contract.
raw: #9 Medium: bulk-deleted flags are not treated as deleted, contradicting the function's documented contract — The docstring states a flag is non-existent if it "was soft-deleted at or before the timestamp (without subsequent restoration)", but `flag_was_deleted` is only updated inside `if version_after is not None` (`:243-250`). The bulk-delete path logs `activity="deleted"` with `Detail(changes=[])` and updates the rows via `queryset.update()` without bumping `version` — so its entries are skipped and the flag is reported as alive for the entire deleted window.

claim: The activity-log window is ordered -created_at and sliced to MAX_HISTORY_ENTRIES, so it keeps the newest entries and silently discards older ones, meaning a `deleted` entry outside the window is never seen by the delete/restore state machine; separately the comment claims .iterator() avoids loading all entries into memory while the code immediately does list(entries).
raw: #10 Low: the entry cap drops the *oldest* entries, and `list(entries)` defeats the streaming the comment claims — The queryset is ordered `-created_at, -id` and then sliced `[:MAX_HISTORY_ENTRIES]` (10 000), so the window keeps the newest entries and silently discards older ones. `most_recent_version` is unaffected, but the delete/restore state machine is: a `deleted` entry that falls outside the window is never seen, and the flag is reported as live. Separately, the comment at `:218-220` says `.iterator()` is used "to avoid loading all entries into memory", and `:235` then does `list(entries)`, materializing up to 10 000 rows including their `detail` JSON.

claim: person_existed_at_timestamp queries events filtered only on team_id, distinct_id and timestamp <= T, with no event-name predicate and no lower time bound, so the negative case must scan every partition for the team and can time out against max_execution_time: 10, surfacing as a 500 instead of the intended 400; it also duplicates rows the properties query re-reads immediately after.
raw: #11 Low: `person_existed_at_timestamp` runs an unfiltered, unbounded `events` scan — The query filters only `team_id`, `distinct_id IN (...)` and `timestamp <= T`, with no event-name predicate and no lower time bound. `distinct_id` is not a leading column of the `events` sort key, so the negative case (no events before `T` — precisely the case this check exists to detect) must scan every partition for the team before returning empty, against `max_execution_time: 10`. On a large team that becomes a timeout, surfacing as the 500 at `feature_flag.py:3455-3460` rather than the intended 400. It also duplicates work.

claim: person_id is declared as a plain CharField and only empty values are rejected before filter(uuid=<value>), so a non-UUID string raises a Django/psycopg error caught by the generic except Exception and returns HTTP 500 "Failed to resolve person" (plus an error-tracking capture) for what is a client input error that should be 400.
raw: #12 Low: an invalid `person_id` produces 500 instead of 400 — `person_id` is a plain `CharField`, and `get_person_and_distinct_ids_for_identifier` only rejects empty values before calling `get_person_by_uuid` → `filter(uuid=<value>)`. A non-UUID string raises a Django/psycopg error, not `ValueError`, so it lands in the generic `except Exception` at `:3414` and returns 500 "Failed to resolve person" for what is plainly a client input error (and the exception is reported to error tracking via `capture_exception`).

claim: TestTimestampBasedReconstruction inherits from the concrete test class TestReconstructFlagAtVersion, so all ~15 parent version-based tests re-run under the new class name, doubling DB setup cost and making failure reports ambiguous.
raw: #13 Low: the new test class inherits `TestReconstructFlagAtVersion`, re-running every parent test — `class TestTimestampBasedReconstruction(TestReconstructFlagAtVersion)` inherits from a concrete `BaseTest` subclass, so all ~15 version-based tests execute a second time under the new class name.
